$comment: One case per playground configuration. `why` writes out the arithmetic a reader would check, exactly as data/golden/vectors.json does for the evaluation engine: a bare expected number is a value somebody typed, and recomputing it in the test from the same annotation would mirror the implementation and prove nothing. content_lint.mjs refuses a case whose why is missing.

cases.why: ph-001 carries 6 objects and 6 annotated edges. Ordered pairs of distinct objects = 6 x 5 = 30. With the slice's 16 predicates the candidate space is 30 x 16 = 480. The annotated share is 6 / 480 = 0.0125.

Same 30 ordered pairs, but with VG-150's 50 predicates: 30 x 50 = 1500. The annotated share is 6 / 1500 = 0.004. This is the vocabulary M0's own worked example computes with, which is why it is offered.

Half of 6 edges is 3. The candidate space does not depend on how many edges were annotated, so it stays 480 and only the numerator moves: 3 / 480 = 0.00625. That the bound does not move is the point of the slider.
No edges kept. 0 / 480 = 0, which is zero and not undefined: the candidate space is non-empty, so the share is a real number.
6 objects give 6 x 5 = 30 ordered pairs of distinct objects, times 16 predicates = 480.
Discarding direction identifies (s,o) with (o,s), so 30 ordered pairs become 15 unordered ones: 15 x 16 = 240, exactly half of 480.
ph-001 relationship 1 is object 3 (box) --on--> object 1 (table). Unswapped, the triplet is the one the annotator wrote, so it is in E.
Swapped, the triplet is table --on--> box. No relationship in ph-001 has subject 1, object 3 and predicate on, so it is not in E. Not in E is not the same claim as false.

ph-001 relationship 2 is object 2 (person) --near--> object 1 (table). `near` reads as symmetric, but the annotator wrote one direction only, so table --near--> person is not in E. This is the case worth showing: the absence is a fact about the annotation, not about the world.
The 80 frames carry 36 predicates. Merging on, above, over and sitting on turns four classes into one: 36 - 4 + 1 = 33. Their triplets add: 382 + 11 + 5 + 10 = 408.
Unmerged, the slice uses 36 predicates, and on alone carries 382 of the 892 triplets. The other three members keep their own 11, 5 and 10.
The slice uses 115 object names. Merging man, person and people turns three into one: 115 - 3 + 1 = 113, with 56 + 52 + 19 = 127 objects in the merged class.
Frame 228, relationship 5 is glass (10) sitting on table (2). The frame carries no on edge from 10 to 2, so glass on table is not in E before the merge.
With on and sitting on merged, glass (10) sitting on table (2) and glass on table share the key (10, on, 2), so the substituted triplet is in E prime. No annotation and no model changed.
At s = 0 every class holds the same count, so the three most frequent of 36 hold 3 / 36 = 1/12 = 0.083333, and the rarest is as frequent as the first: 36^0 = 1.
H_4 at s = 1 is 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 = 25/12. The first class holds 1 / (25/12) = 12/25 = 0.48. The fourth is 4^(-1) = 0.25 of the first.
The slice's three most frequent predicates are on 382, has 68 and near 59: 382 + 68 + 59 = 509 of 892 triplets, and 509 / 892 = 0.570628.
v2 states 68,538 training images and the canonical protocol 57,723: 68,538 - 57,723 = 10,815, which is the card's own count of v2 training images kept with no relation.
v2 states 31,876 test images and the canonical protocol 26,446: 31,876 - 26,446 = 5,430, the card's count of v2 test images kept with no relation.
Issue 94 gives v1 73,538 training images against v2's 68,538: 73,538 - 68,538 = 5,000, the canonical validation set the card says v1 folded into train.
v1 has 27,032 test images and v2 31,876: 27,032 - 31,876 = -4,844. The 4,844 are the images the card says v1 took from the test pool for its validation set.
Xu et al. state 70% of 108,077 images and no count, so there is no count to subtract from 57,723. Multiplying 0.7 by 108,077 would assert a split size the paper never states.
